title: Two hold a cloak (Bava Metzia 2a)
hook: two people claim one garment; each swears, and they divide it
tomorrow: A court that almost never executed

segments.voice: Yesterday, hashavat aveidah, returning a lost thing, and the line from Deuteronomy about not hiding yourself. Your line was return it. Did something find its way home? Day one thousand eighty-three.

One cloak, and two fists closed on it. Not tugging. Just holding. One says: I found it. The other says: I found it. One says: it's all mine. The other says: it's all mine. There are no witnesses, no receipt, and no window into either heart. This is the case that opens the tractate Bava Metzia, the middle gate of the laws of damages and dealings. Today: what a court does when both stories sound exactly the same.
screen: `ONE CLOAK, TWO FISTS.` → `I FOUND IT. I FOUND IT.` → `NO WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Two hold a cloak. The Mishnah's ruling is short. Each one swears that they own no less than half of it, and they divide. Look at what that oath does. Neither swears it's all theirs. Each swears only to the part that could be true for both of them at once. The court doesn't pretend to know what it can't know. It takes each claim at the size it can trust, and cuts there. Then the Mishnah changes the case. One says, it's all mine. The other says, half of it is mine. Now the first swears to no less than three quarters, and the second to no less than a quarter. Work it through. The one claiming half has already granted the other half. Only one half is really in dispute, so only that half gets split. The rule isn't split everything down the middle. It's split what's actually contested. The Talmud lingers over these few lines. One question it asks: if they're dividing anyway, why make anyone swear? One answer it gives: so that nobody grabs a stranger's cloak in the street, says it's mine, and hopes to walk off with half. The oath makes a grab cost something. Read the case once more and three pieces of a fair process show through. Hear both sides as equals. Divide only what's truly in dispute. Make lying expensive. And none of it depends on knowing who's right. That's the honest part. A court that admits what it can't see.
screen: `EACH SWEARS: NO LESS THAN HALF.` · `ALL VERSUS HALF: THREE QUARTERS, ONE QUARTER.` · `SPLIT ONLY WHAT'S CONTESTED.` · `THE OATH MAKES A GRAB COST SOMETHING.` · then, large: `EACH TAKES HALF.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: settle a disagreement fairly, starting in your head. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one small dispute that's still open. Whose turn it is. Who said what. Whose idea it was. Hold it the way the court holds the cloak, with both fists on it at once. What does the other person actually claim? What have they already granted you, and what have you granted them? Find the piece that's truly contested, and let the rest go. Notice how much smaller it is than the whole. The bell holds the time.
Two hold a cloak. The opening case of Bava Metzia: two claim one garment, each swears to no less than half, and they divide. Today's word.
Your line: each takes half. Today, when a disagreement comes up, find the part both of you could be right about, and split only what's left. Day one thousand eighty-three.
